reading.title: Hanging, Weighing, and Spending
reading.purpose: Discover how one Latin root connects swinging weights, quiet thinking, and paying out.
paras: A single Latin root, pend or pens, hides inside dozens of English words. Long ago, it meant both "to hang" and "to weigh," because merchants weighed coins on hanging balance scales. Once you know that picture, a whole family of words clicks into place.

Start with things that literally hang. A pendant is a charm or stone that dangles from a necklace chain. Inside a tall clock, a pendulum swings steadily back and forth from a fixed rod. When builders suspend a bridge from thick cables, they hang the roadway in the air. Even a book's appendix hangs on at the very end, adding extra charts or notes after the final chapter.

The root also describes events and feelings that seem to hang overhead. An impending storm is one about to arrive soon, like dark clouds poised above a field. When you depend on a friend, you rely on that person's support. A pensive traveler sits quiet and deep in thought, mentally weighing choices on an invisible scale.

Finally, the weighing side of the root gave us words about money and effort. To expend energy means to use it up while working or playing hard. A machine can dispense soap or tickets in measured amounts, just as a shopkeeper once weighed out goods. If a store makes a mistake, it may compensate a customer by giving something back to balance the loss.

Next time you meet an unfamiliar word with pend or pens, pause and picture that hanging scale. Ask whether something is dangling, waiting overhead, or being weighed out, and the meaning often becomes clear.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "pensive" most nearly means
choices: eager to spend money quickly at a busy market
quiet and deep in thought while weighing ideas
worried about an approaching rainstorm outdoors
hanging loosely from a fixed rod or metal chain
qs.why: Paragraph 3 describes a pensive traveler as "quiet and deep in thought, mentally weighing choices."

qs.q: Which sentence explains why the Latin root meant both "to hang" and "to weigh"?
choices: A single Latin root, pend or pens, hides inside dozens of English words.
Once you know that picture, a whole family of words clicks into place.
Long ago, it meant both "to hang" and "to weigh," because merchants weighed coins on hanging balance scales.
When builders suspend a bridge from thick cables, they hang the roadway in the air.
qs.why: This sentence directly links the two meanings through merchants weighing coins on hanging scales.

ev.text: Long ago, it meant both "to hang" and "to weigh," because merchants weighed coins on hanging balance scales.

qs.q: How is compensating a customer like using a balance scale?
choices: Both require hanging a heavy weight from a tall wooden clock.
Both involve adding something back so a loss is made even again.
Both happen only when a traveler sits quietly and thinks about choices.
Both depend on extra charts printed after the final chapter of a book.
qs.why: Paragraph 4 says to compensate is to give something back "to balance the loss," just like evening out a scale.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Knowing the root pend/pens helps readers unlock many English words.
Ancient merchants invented the first tall clocks and necklace chains.
Most modern machines dispense soap and tickets without using scales.
Every English word about books or storms comes from ancient coins.
qs.why: Each paragraph shows a branch of the pend/pens family, and the ending explains how picturing the hanging scale reveals word meanings.

clues.text: a charm or stone that dangles from a necklace chain
to use it up while working or playing hard

reading.retellFrame: Because the Latin root pend/pens means ___, it connects words like ___ and ___.
